title: How Many Categories Are Enough? Distribution-Free Certification Limits for Few-Shot Anomaly Thresholds

paper.title: How Many Categories Are Enough? Distribution-Free Certification Limits for Few-Shot Anomaly Thresholds
paper.abstract: Abstract Few-shot anomaly detectors are judged by ranking metrics, yet deployment requires an alarm threshold with a controlled false-alarm rate (FAR). We ask how much normal evidence, in images or category units, is needed to certify such a threshold for an unseen category. Using a frozen DINOv2 principal component analysis (PCA) residual ranker on 15 MVTec and 12 VisA categories under four corruption types, we show that target-only leave-one-image-out (LOIO) calibration is resolution-limited and shift-fragile: rank values cannot fall below 1 / ( k + 1 ) 1/(k+1) , and at the attainable level α = 0.20 \alpha=0.20 , empirical FAR reaches 0.341 on Gaussian-corrupted MVTec at k = 4 k=4 , 1.7 times the nominal level. A category-count feasibility calculus is then derived: even with all-zero category losses and no multiplicity charged, any deterministic, uniformly valid, distribution-free 95% upper confidence bound (UCB) requires at least 14, 29, and 59 independent and identically distributed (iid) category draws at α = 0.20 \alpha=0.20 , 0.10 0.10 , and 0.05 0.05 ; these counts are necessary but not sufficient. The Cross-category Reliability Estimation with Source Support (CRESS) protocol splits source categories into disjoint reference, proposal, and certification roles. With only three or four certification categories, all 960 frozen configurations return the fail-closed threshold τ ⋆ = 0 \tau^{\star}=0 , and the smallest category-level UCB is 0.950. Image-unit analyses of the same archive select positive thresholds in 36.7% to 60.3% of target cells; these bounds hold for the selected source mixture, not for the marginal risk of a new-category draw. The contribution is a quantitative feasibility boundary and an estimand-aware protocol specifying when source evidence can, and cannot, support a transferable reliability claim.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: At the nominal false-alarm level α = 0.20 \alpha=0.20 , the target-only alarm evaluated in this study achieves an empirical false-alarm rate (FAR) of 0.341 on Gaussian-corrupted MVTec at k = 4 k=4 . This value represents the largest dataset-level aggregate in the frozen corruption grid and is approximately 1.7 times the intended level. This figure does not represent a population-level failure probability; rather, it is a benchmark observation pooled across categories and five support-sampling seeds under a single declared synthetic shift. However, this result highlights an operational discrepancy that ranking metrics alone do not capture. A detector may assign higher anomaly scores to defects than to normal images, resulting in a strong area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) or average precision (AP), yet a fixed score threshold can still yield substantially different false-alarm behavior across categories or input conditions. This discrepancy is especially significant in few-shot industrial anomaly detection (AD). Typically, a target category provides only k ∈ { 1 , 2 , 4 , 8 } k\in\{1,2,4,8\} known-normal support images, while anomalous examples are rare, heterogeneous, and unavailable for threshold calibration. Frozen visual foundation models enable ranking in this context: DINOv2 [ 24 ] patch features support nearest-neighbor (NN) memory banks, as implemented in PatchCore-style methods and AnomalyDINO [ 27 , 7 ] , or compact principal component analysis (PCA) normal subspaces, as in SubspaceAD [ 20 ] . However, these advances do not inherently determine which alarm threshold possesses a stable operational interpretation. Two primary responses are possible. The first is to calibrate on the k k target-normal support images. The target-only method evaluates each support image using a leave-one-image-out (LOIO) fit and ranks a test score against the resulting normal scores. This approach is label-free and interpretable, but its rank values are restricted to the grid { j / ( k + 1 ) } \{j/(k+1)\} . Increasing k k refines this grid; however, it does not guarantee that the support and shifted test scores meet the exchangeability conditions required for false-alarm validity. The empirical FAR of 0.341 illustrates this distinction: while the operating level is achievable, the shifted-normal rank distribution is anti-conservative compared to the exchangeable reference. The second approach involves leveraging normal evidence from non-target source categories. A larger source archive provides finer empirical ranks and enables the proposal of thresholds below those available in the target-only grid. However, this strategy alters the underlying statistical question. Independent image samples from a specified source mixture can estimate risk for that mixture, whereas a guarantee for a previously unseen category requires independent and identically distributed (iid) category units from a defined meta-population. Repeated images, corruption views, or support seeds do not constitute new category units. Consequently, the central question addressed in this paper is: How much source evidence, measured in which statistical unit, is needed to certify an anomaly threshold for a new category? We address this question at three levels. First, for any deterministic, uniformly valid, distribution-free 95% upper confidence bound (UCB) based solely on independent and identically distributed (iid) category losses, an all-zero sample cannot certify α = 0.20 \alpha=0.20 , 0.10, or 0.05 with fewer than 14, 29, or 59 categories, respectively, even without multiplicity. These values represent optimistic impossibility limits rather than sufficient sample sizes for the procedure. Under frozen simultaneous allocation, the corresponding lower limits are at least 22, 46, and 94 for a single candidate, while the declared Hoeffding rule requires 60, 240, and 958 categories, respectively. Second, we audit target-only normal rank values under four controlled corruptions and demonstrate that crossing the finite resolution floor does not guarantee a stable FAR. Third, we employ CRESS to partition source categories into disjoint reference, threshold-proposal, and certification roles and assess whether the available archive achieves the predicted feasibility boundary. CRESS functions as a source-assisted thresholding and audit protocol rather than as a novel anomaly ranker. The inherited ranking substrate is a frozen DINOv2 PCA residual. The reference categories establish a source-reference rank map, proposal categories define a finite candidate set, and certification categories evaluate fixed candidates using a family-adjusted UCB. The protocol outputs either the largest passing threshold or the fail-closed value of zero. Source-risk dominance enables the transfer of the bound to a specific target category. An iid category-sampling model provides only a marginal bound averaged over a new-category draw, rather than category-conditional control for each realized target. Neither normalization nor source pooling satisfies these requirements. The strict audit includes only three certification categories in VisA cells and four in MVTec and transfer cells. This limitation is not solely attributable to the fixed 0.50 / 0.25 / 0.25 0.50/0.25/0.25 split. The eligible source pools contain 11, 14, or 15 categories. Maintaining nonempty reference and proposal roles restricts certification categories to at most 9, 12, or 13, all below the optimistic 14-category threshold at α = 0.20 \alpha=0.20 . Consequently, category-unit certification assigns τ ⋆ = 0 \tau^{\star}=0 to every target cell across the 960 frozen configurations. This outcome does not represent 960 independent failures or a computational or optimization failure. The configurations cover various jobs, source-view modes, support sizes, nominal levels, and conditions but share the same category-count obstruction. Their value is to show that the fail-closed outcome persists throughout the declared grid in the regime where analytic calculations predict infeasibility. In contrast, under the idealized iid source-image model, image-unit analyses include 72 to 191 units per cell and select positive thresholds in 36.7% to 60.3% of target cells, depending on the source-to-target job. This contrast does not reflect a simple stronger-versus-weaker certificate; rather, the two analyses address different risk profiles. The same source archive is statistically large when measured in images but insufficient when deployment is considered at the category level. This paper presents three primary contributions: • A category-count feasibility calculus. The Hoeffding-specific requirement and a broader all-zero lower bound for deterministic uniformly valid distribution-free category-risk upper bounds are derived. These calculations quantify the minimum budget of iid category draws implied by the requested risk and confidence levels, serving as a study-design tool rather than solely a post hoc explanation. • An operational shift audit. Across 15 MVTec and 12 VisA categories, the target-only analysis distinguishes unattainable nominal levels from attainable but unstable operating points. The largest dataset-level aggregate FAR is 0.341 on Gaussian-corrupted MVTec at k = 4 k=4 and α = 0.20 \alpha=0.20 . VisA demonstrates conservative behavior in the corresponding cells, indicating that the shift effect is dataset-dependent rather than universal. • An estimand-aware source protocol. The CRESS protocol separates reference, proposal, and certification categories, retains zero fallbacks, and reports image-mixture and category-level conclusions without substituting one for the other. The frozen strict audit verifies the predicted category shortage within datasets and for transfer from MVTec to VisA and the Metal Parts Defect Dataset (MPDD). Direct pooling and compact-ranker results are reported solely as supporting empirical context. Figure 1 previews the central design calculation. The black curve represents the optimistic multiplicity-free floor for deterministic uniformly valid distribution-free bounds within the scope of Proposition 3. The blue and orange curves incorporate the frozen family allocation and the declared Hoeffding rule in their most favorable one-candidate case. A positive certificate is infeasible within the corresponding rule class whenever its curve remains above the requested α \alpha . The shaded region indicates the three or four certification categories available in the strict audit. Table 1 subsequently reports the exact candidate-family calculations. Figure 1: Analytic category-count feasibility after observing zero loss in every certification category. The black curve is the multiplicity-free lower bound 1 − 0.05 1 / n 1-0.05^{1/n} for deterministic uniformly valid distribution-free procedures in Proposition 3. The blue curve applies the frozen allocation β = δ / ( 2 ​ A ​ M ) \beta=\delta/(2AM) with δ = 0.05 \delta=0.05 , A = 3 A=3 reported levels, and the favorable one-candidate case M = 1 M=1 ; the orange curve is the corresponding Hoeffding floor. Horizontal lines mark the requested risk levels, and the shaded region marks the three or four distinct certification categories available in the frozen audit; interpreting them as iid units is a modeling assumption. The black circular crossings at the 14, 29, and 59 axis ticks mark optimistic necessary counts without multiplicity, not sufficient sample sizes for CRESS. A curve above a requested α \alpha rules out a positive threshold only within its stated procedure class, even under all-zero observed category loss. The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. Section 2 positions the study against few-shot detectors, calibration, and conformal risk control. Section 3 defines the inherited scorer, target-only route, source construction, CRESS protocol, and certificate scope. Section 4 specifies the frozen datasets, statistical units, partitions, and claim rules. Section 5 presents the shift audit, category-count feasibility, and strict CRESS, followed by supporting ranking and storage analysis. Sections 6 and 7 outline the study’s boundaries and implications.

sections.heading: 2.1 Few-Shot Industrial AD
sections.text: Classical industrial AD typically assumed access to normal-only training data and identified deviations at test time. Patch distribution, self-supervised, and reconstruction-discriminative approaches such as PaDiM, CutPaste, and DRAEM provided important context for this literature [ 8 , 21 , 35 ] . PatchCore [ 27 ] established memory-bank patch retrieval as a robust baseline by storing representative normal features and scoring test patches using NN distance. AnomalyDINO [ 7 ] extended this paradigm to few-shot inspection with frozen DINOv2 representations. Subsequent work introduced registration-based adaptation (RegAD [ 15 ] ), graph-structured memory (GraphCore [ 32 ] ), and fast feature reconstruction (FastRecon [ 9 ] ). Vision-language methods included WinCLIP [ 16 ] , CLIP-SAM collaboration [ 22 ] , and cross-modal prompt regularization [ 31 ] . InCTRL introduced in-context residual learning [ 36 ] . These methods were effective rankers; however, their raw score scales did not, by construction, provide a certified false-alarm rate interpretation. Calibration under distribution shift is also known to degrade for deep models in general [ 25 ] . The present work is complementary: rather than competing on ranking, it examines how few-shot detectors should expose decision reliability.

sections.heading: 2.2 Frozen-Feature Subspace Detectors
sections.text: Subspace approaches replaced explicit patch retrieval with a compact normal subspace. SubspaceAD [ 20 ] demonstrated that frozen DINOv2 patch features and PCA or subspace residuals were already effective for few-shot anomaly ranking, establishing the ranking mechanism as prior art. The present contribution begins after computing the residual and examines the reliability claims that a low-storage subspace detector can support under few-shot and distribution-shift conditions.

sections.heading: 2.3 Calibration and Decision Reliability in Few-Shot AD
sections.text: Calibration measured agreement between predicted confidence and empirical correctness [ 26 , 11 ] . Standard post-hoc methods included Platt scaling and temperature scaling [ 26 , 11 ] . Histogram binning and isotonic regression provided nonparametric alternatives [ 33 , 34 ] . Sparse labels, open-ended anomaly types, and category-dependent scores made this objective especially difficult in AD. Prior reliability analyses of few-shot AD based on DINOv2 have also documented calibration and perturbation sensitivity [ 17 ] . These findings motivated our separation of ranking quality from the operational question of whether a declared alarm rule maintains its requested false-alarm behavior under a specified shift. A calibrated probability summary alone would not constitute such a risk guarantee.

sections.heading: 2.4 Conformal Prediction and Risk-Controlled Calibration
sections.text: Conformal prediction transformed nonconformity scores into p-values under exchangeability assumptions [ 30 , 28 , 1 ] . This approach was particularly well suited for normal-only few-shot AD because normal support images defined a reference distribution without needing real anomalies. The literature on conformal AD was well established. Leave-one-out, bootstrap, and cross-conformal anomaly detectors had been directly analyzed [ 13 ] . Weighted conformal detection in low-data regimes examined the effects of resolution and effective sample size [ 14 ] . General nonconformity toolkits had been developed [ 12 ] . Few-shot conformal prediction with auxiliary tasks addressed the challenge of small target calibration sets [ 10 ] . Conformal AD, LOIO calibration, auxiliary-task transfer, and weighted conformal p-values were therefore established mechanisms. Risk-controlling calibration methods were developed before this work. The Learn then Test framework formulated finite-sample calibration as a multiple-testing problem over candidate configurations [ 2 ] . Conformal risk control selected parameters to control the expectation of a monotone loss [ 3 ] . In anomaly detection, PAC-Wrap provided semi-supervised probably approximately correct (PAC) bounds for false-positive and false-negative rates around a base detector [ 23 ] . These studies established general principles of candidate testing, held-out risk assessment, and one-sided error bounds. This work does not claim those statistical primitives as novel. Instead, CRESS applies these principles for normal-only cross-category thresholding by assigning disjoint source categories to reference, proposal, and certification roles. It distinguishes selected-mixture image risk from marginal new-category risk and audits whether the available category count can support a nonzero threshold under the declared iid model. Structure-aware conformal adaptation has also been studied outside the context of anomaly detection. Lam and Anh proposed Heterophily-Aware Diffused Conformal Prediction (HeAD-CP), which adapted graph-score diffusion using label-free local homophily estimates and showed that uniform diffusion could impair prediction-set efficiency on heterophilic graphs while preserving marginal coverage [ 18 ] . This result supported the broader need to audit reliability transformations under structural shift; however, its setting concerned graph neural network (GNN) node-classification sets rather than few-shot industrial anomaly alarms or cross-category source certification. The deterministic source-view choices were conceptually informed by the shared-versus-specialized selection motif in Shape-Adapting Gated Experts (SAGE) [ 29 ] . That work concerned learned expert selection rather than certification of anomaly thresholds. CRESS does not use a learned expert gate; its source-view modes are predeclared protocol choices, and its reference, proposal, and certification partitions have disjoint statistical roles. The citation therefore records design inspiration without attributing CRESS validity or novelty to the SAGE architecture. This contribution begins with the independent-category requirement of a simultaneous source certificate, using the target-only grid 1 / ( k + 1 ) 1/(k{+}1) as a motivating finite-resolution constraint. Established confidence tools are specialized into Hoeffding-specific and distribution-free all-zero category-budget calculations. Corruption-shift deviations are empirically audited. Source-assisted candidate thresholds are evaluated without target anomaly labels. CRESS does not introduce a new nonconformity score or generic confidence bound. Instead, it specifies the separation of source categories into reference, proposal, and certification roles and audits whether the resulting source certificate can be nonvacuous at the available category count.

sections.heading: 3.1 Problem Setup
sections.text: For each target category c c , a support set 𝒮 c = { x i } i = 1 k \mathcal{S}_{c}=\{x_{i}\}_{i=1}^{k} consisting solely of normal images is observed. Target test images may be either normal or anomalous, but their labels are reserved exclusively for evaluation and are not utilized in detector fitting, threshold proposal, or certification. Other categories may additionally provide a declared source-normal archive. The framework outputs a fixed raw anomaly score s c ​ ( x ) s_{c}(x) and an optional pixel map, a target-only reliability value p LOIO ​ ( x ) p_{\mathrm{LOIO}}(x) when LOIO calibration is available, and, for the source-assisted route, a threshold τ ⋆ \tau^{\star} with an accompanying source-domain certificate. Figures 2 and 3 distinguish the inherited ranking substrate, the target-only route, and the source-assisted route. The statistical unit is fixed before threshold evaluation. Under the idealized iid image model, image-unit analysis gives equal weight to each retained source image and targets the mean alarm loss for a sample drawn from the induced source-image mixture, where category weights are proportional to the number of retained images. In contrast, category-unit analysis first averages alarms within each source category, gives equal weight to each certification category, and then targets the expected archive-level loss for a new sample from the declared source-category meta-population. In this context, a category unit consists of the category, its support-set construction, and its predeclared held-out normal-view sampling mechanism. To equate this expectation with the alarm probability of a fresh normal image, the within-category views must be representative of the declared deployment distribution. Independent category units remain necessary; additional images, support seeds, or corruption views within an existing category do not increase the number of units. Neither source estimand directly corresponds to the target-category risk. Achieving this transfer requires the additional condition specified at the end of this section.

sections.heading: 4.1 Datasets and Few-Shot Splits
sections.text: MVTec AD [ 6 ] and VisA [ 37 ] are evaluated in this study. The strict external-transfer audit also incorporates MPDD. MVTec AD includes industrial object and texture categories with pixel-level defect masks. VisA encompasses a broader range of industrial categories and serves as the primary benchmark for full-scale corruption and calibration shift. MPDD provides six metal-part categories for an external stress test that transfers from MVTec to MPDD. Within-MPDD certification is not conducted because the frozen nested implementation requires at least six eligible source categories, and excluding one MPDD target leaves only five. For each category and seed, a random permutation of the path-sorted normal training images defines nested support sets, ensuring that the k k -shot set is contained within every larger declared set. The CRESS source archive is maintained separately and consists of held-out known-normal evaluation images from non-target source categories (the test/good partition for MVTec and the corresponding normal partition for VisA and MPDD). Source normal status is used, but target test labels are never included in reference construction, threshold proposal, or certification. Unless otherwise specified, k ∈ { 1 , 2 , 4 , 8 } k\in\{1,2,4,8\} is used for the clean accuracy-storage and strict nested studies, while the target-only corruption tables use k ∈ { 4 , 8 } k\in\{4,8\} . The k = 1 k=1 strict cells employ the declared patch-split support calibration fallback and are interpreted as stress tests; LOIO calibration requires k ≥ 2 k\geq 2 .

sections.heading: 4.2 Evaluation Protocols
sections.text: The target-only corruption audit evaluates all test images from 15 MVTec and 12 VisA categories at k ∈ { 4 , 8 } k\in\{4,8\} under five support-sampling seeds, with the k k sets nested within each seed and four corruption types. Support images remain clean, and each corruption is applied only to evaluation views. Images are represented on [ 0 , 1 ] [0,1] . Gaussian noise introduces independent 𝒩 ⁡ ( 0 , 0.05 2 ) \mathcal{N}(0,0.05^{2}) pixel-channel noise and clips the result. Blur is implemented using a box-filter radius of one pixel, corresponding to the declared three-pixel kernel. Brightness and contrast adjustments apply clip ⁡ ( 1.15 ​ ( x − 0.5 ) + 0.55 , 0 , 1 ) \operatorname{clip}(1.15(x-0.5)+0.55,0,1) . JPEG corruption uses a quality-60 encode/decode process. Each transformed array is clipped, quantized to 8-bit, and stored as a PNG before feature extraction. The noise generator uses the support seed plus the fixed image index, while the other transformations are deterministic. Primary rank values follow Equation ( 4 ): calibration scores use LOIO fits, and each test score uses the full-support fit. The fold-matched construction is reported only as a sensitivity analysis. Alarm comparisons use the predeclared tolerance 10 − 6 10^{-6} to absorb fp32 representation error at attainable grid points. The primary empirical groups include the target-only corruption audit and the frozen strict nested CRESS audit, while the category-count feasibility curves are based on analytic design calculations. Supporting groups address clean ranking and storage, PCA64/PCA128 sensitivity, direct pooled-source conformal, and attainable operating levels. The strict nested protocol employs k ∈ { 1 , 2 , 4 , 8 } k\in\{1,2,4,8\} , seeds from 0 to 4, α ∈ { 0.05 , 0.10 , 0.20 } \alpha\in\{0.05,0.10,0.20\} , and clean, Gaussian-noise, blur, brightness/contrast, and JPEG conditions. The shared score export retains at most 120 evaluation records per category, seed, and condition through deterministic label-stratified sampling, with dataset labels determining the retained evaluation strata. Target labels are used only to score evaluation outcomes and do not enter threshold construction. Downstream source construction discards every anomalous source row, so source anomaly scores are excluded from the reference map, proposal, and certification losses. The remaining cells use ρ = 0.01 \rho=0.01 , PCA64, δ = 0.05 \delta=0.05 , and realized M = | 𝒯 | ≤ 20 M=|\mathcal{T}|\leq 20 . Raw scores are first normalized using support-only statistics, and condition-specific source views are then selected or aggregated as defined in Section 3.5 . For each target category and seed, eligible source categories are deterministically split using the frozen 0.50 / 0.25 / 0.25 0.50/0.25/0.25 reference/proposal/certification allocation. This results in 7/3/4 categories for a 14-category within-MVTec source pool, 5/3/3 for an 11-category within-VisA pool, and 7/4/4 for the 15-category MVTec transfer pool. The same category partition is reused across conditions and k k . The protocol evaluates MVTec and VisA within-dataset, MVTec-to-VisA, and MVTec-to-MPDD under matched-condition, clean-source, condition-agnostic, and mismatched negative-control source selection. The frozen operational gate requires a positive category-level threshold in at least 80% of target cells. It subsequently checks target FAR, power, no-harm relative to LOIO, and power gain below the target-only floor. The 80% cutoff serves as a predeclared usability criterion rather than a confidence level; since the observed rate is zero, any positive cutoff yields the same verdict. The confidence allocation described in Proposition 1 applies within each fixed target, seed, source-view mode, and condition cell, but does not constitute a simultaneous 95% guarantee over the entire experimental grid. Failed cells are retained.

sections.heading: 4.3 Baselines and Ablations
sections.text: The inherited PCA residual scorer is compared with a controlled nearest-neighbor memory bank, both using the same frozen DINOv2 features and few-shot split. PCA64 and PCA128 retain 64 and 128 principal directions, respectively, with PCA64 serving as the default reliability substrate. In the source-assisted study, direct pooled-source conformal serves as an uncertified baseline; it employs the complete selected source pool with τ = α \tau=\alpha , but does not perform reference, proposal, or certification splits and does not apply a UCB gate. The controlled memory-bank implementation is not an official reproduction of PatchCore or AnomalyDINO, but instead isolates scoring and storage trade-offs under a unified protocol. AnomalyDINO-S (448) [ 7 ] is included based on values reported under its published protocol. WinCLIP [ 16 ] is also included only through published values, as the audit identifies no author-released implementation associated with the cited paper. SubspaceAD is treated as a prior-art guardrail rather than a controlled baseline; the frozen DINOv2 subspace residual is inherited, and the contribution begins with the reliability analysis downstream of that score.

sections.heading: 4.4 Metrics
sections.text: Ranking metrics are distinguished from reliability metrics. Image AUROC and AP are calculated from the raw PCA residual score s ⁡ ( x ) s(x) ; pixel maps are not considered certification targets. Reliability is evaluated operationally by empirical FAR at fixed α \alpha , detection power, alarm precision, the empirical cumulative distribution function (CDF) of normal rank values, and the fraction of cells receiving a positive certified threshold. Storage is quantified as retained ranker state per category. Corruption views serve as controlled stress tests and are not treated as independent images or as proxies for all deployment shifts.

sections.heading: Category-level residual-displacement analysis.
sections.text: To examine the difference between MVTec and VisA without treating images or support seeds as independent replications, a paired category-level analysis is conducted using only normal evaluation images. For category c c , support seed r r , and corruption q q , each corrupted view is paired with its corresponding clean base image. The residual displacement is defined as Δ ​ s c , r , q = median x ⁡ log ⁡ s c , r ​ ( x q ) + ϵ s c , r ​ ( x clean ) + ϵ , \Delta s_{c,r,q}=\operatorname{median}_{x}\log\frac{s_{c,r}(x^{q})+\epsilon}{s_{c,r}(x^{\mathrm{clean}})+\epsilon}, where ϵ = 10 − 12 \epsilon=10^{-12} denotes a fixed numerical stabilizer. Since the paired views share identical support-derived calibration scores, this quantity measures corruption-induced movement relative to a fixed calibration reference and avoids comparisons of absolute residual scales across categories. The corresponding FAR inflation is Δ ​ FAR c , r , q = FAR c , r , q − FAR c , r , clean . \Delta\mathrm{FAR}_{c,r,q}=\mathrm{FAR}_{c,r,q}-\mathrm{FAR}_{c,r,\mathrm{clean}}. Both quantities are averaged over the five support seeds prior to computing Spearman’s rank correlation across categories, separately for each dataset, k k , and corruption. Categories, rather than images or seeds, serve as the analysis units. The correlations are descriptive and are not interpreted as causal relationships.

sections.heading: 4.5 Reproducibility and Claim Rules
sections.text: All experiments are conducted on a single NVIDIA RTX 5090 graphics processing unit (GPU) using PyTorch 2.12.1. DINOv2 patch features are cached in 32-bit floating-point (fp32) format. Reproducibility records include the declared protocol revision, recorded worktree state, DINOv2 source-tree and weight hashes, environment specifications, dataset counts, per-image predictions, base-image identities, support manifests, corruption parameters, source partitions, candidate-threshold bounds, and Secure Hash Algorithm 256-bit (SHA-256) checksums. Automated integrity checks are performed for 1,500 MVTec, 1,200 VisA, and 600 MPDD view cells, rejecting duplicate cells, missing support statistics, or overlap between support and test sets. Reliability methods cannot claim ranking improvement unless the raw score is altered; image-level and category-level certificates are not interchangeable.

sections.heading: 5.2 Category-Level Residual Displacement
sections.text: The paired analysis establishes a relationship between dataset-level FAR contrast and the displacement of normal residual scores. In the MVTec dataset, both Gaussian noise and JPEG compression result in systematic positive shifts in scores. At k = 4 k=4 , the category-level Spearman correlations between residual displacement and FAR inflation are ρ = 0.825 \rho=0.825 for Gaussian noise and ρ = 0.875 \rho=0.875 for JPEG. At k = 8 k=8 , these correlations increase to 0.843 0.843 and 0.914 0.914 , respectively. The corresponding median log-score displacements are 0.037 and 0.025 at k = 4 k=4 , and 0.042 and 0.027 at k = 8 k=8 . Median FAR inflation exhibits a similar trend: 0.033 and 0.036 at k = 4 k=4 , and 0.067 and 0.050 at k = 8 k=8 . In contrast, the VisA dataset does not demonstrate a comparable dataset-wide displacement. For both Gaussian noise and JPEG compression, the median log-score shifts are approximately 0.000 and 0.004 at both support sizes. Median FAR changes are − 0.003 -0.003 and − 0.005 -0.005 at k = 4 k=4 , and − 0.007 -0.007 and 0.002 at k = 8 k=8 . Within VisA, the category-level correlations remain positive, suggesting that categories with greater score displacement tend to exhibit larger FAR changes. However, both metrics remain centered near zero at the dataset level. These results support residual displacement as a proximal explanation for the observed FAR behavior. In MVTec, normal scores increase systematically under Gaussian noise and JPEG compression, whereas VisA normal scores exhibit minimal aggregate movement. The analysis does not address the underlying reasons for the differing responses of the frozen representation across datasets, nor does it establish a causal relationship with dataset composition. Since FAR is determined by thresholding ranks derived from the same residual scores, the observed correlation is partly structural. Its primary value lies in demonstrating that the aggregate contrast is distributed across categories and aligns with measurable score displacement, rather than being attributable to a single category.

sections.heading: 5.3 Category-Count Feasibility
sections.text: Figure 1 and Table 1 present analytic design calculations rather than fitted learning curves. In the optimistic scenario without multiplicity, the all-zero distribution-free floor intersects α = 0.20 \alpha=0.20 , 0.10, and 0.05 at 14, 29, and 59 iid category draws. These counts are necessary under Proposition 3 but are not sufficient to achieve a positive CRESS threshold. Using the frozen family allocation with A = 3 A=3 and favorable M = 1 M=1 , the lower limits increase to 22, 46, and 94, while the Hoeffding rule requires 60, 240, and 958 draws. The presence of candidate multiplicity further increases the required sample sizes. With the cap at M = 20 M=20 , the family-adjusted distribution-free lower limits rise to 35, 74, and 152, while the Hoeffding requirements increase to 98, 390, and 1,557. The three or four certification categories available in the frozen audit remain below even the most optimistic 14-category requirement at α = 0.20 \alpha=0.20 . This limitation is not solely due to allocating 25% of the source pool to certification. Any disjoint split with nonempty reference and proposal roles can allocate at most 12 MVTec, 9 VisA, or 13 transfer-source categories to certification, all below 14. This comparison addresses a feasibility question before evaluating target performance. Within the deterministic distribution-free framework of Proposition 3, a nonzero certificate of marginal new-category risk cannot be obtained from the current source pools, even when no category loss is observed. However, this result does not preclude parametric, hierarchical, randomized, or side-information-based procedures, which require separate assumptions and validity justifications. The confidence-level perspective further illustrates the insufficiency. At α = 0.20 \alpha=0.20 , three all-zero categories provide a maximum of 48.8% confidence, while four categories provide up to 59.0% confidence under the optimistic multiplicity-free assumptions of Proposition 3. If a 95% confidence level is required, the corresponding all-zero UCB floors are 0.632 and 0.527, respectively. Both values significantly exceed 0.20, even before accounting for candidate multiplicity or image-unit co-reporting.

sections.heading: 6 Limitations
sections.text: The guarantees apply within a defined statistical scope. Proposition 3 addresses deterministic, uniformly valid, distribution free UCBs based only on iid bounded category losses. The counts 14, 29, and 59 represent optimistic necessary limits without accounting for multiplicity, and do not constitute sufficient CRESS budgets. Methods utilizing pre-specified parametric or hierarchical models, informative auxiliary data, or randomized procedures may function with fewer categories, but each requires a distinct validity analysis. Proposition 1 governs the declared candidate family within a single fixed experimental cell and does not claim a single simultaneous 95% event across the entire reported grid. The empirical conclusions are directly linked to the specified sampling unit and benchmark scope. At the category level, interpretation considers entire category units, including support construction and held-out views, as iid samples from a defined meta-population. In contrast, image-unit sensitivity focuses on the selected mixture of source images. Successful transfer to a realized target further requires source-risk dominance, whereas sampling from the same meta-population supports only marginal statements about new categories. The audit encompasses MVTec, VisA, MPDD, and four controlled corruptions, rather than the full spectrum of production shifts. The frozen DINOv2 PCA residual serves as an inherited ranking substrate, not as a new state-of-the-art ranker. These limitations underscore the need for validation on category-rich source archives and anticipated operational shifts, as well as for assumption-aware alternatives to the distribution-free bounds examined in this study.

sections.heading: 7 Conclusion and Future Work
sections.text: This study has established that the reliability of few-shot anomaly thresholds depends on both the amount and the statistical unit of normal evidence. At nominal α = 0.20 \alpha=0.20 , the target-only LOIO audit has yielded an empirical FAR of 0.341 on Gaussian-corrupted MVTec at k = 4 k=4 , showing that an attainable operating point need not remain stable under shift. The finite floor 1 / ( k + 1 ) 1/(k+1) has explained when a target-only rule is structurally silent, while the shift audit has shown that crossing this floor does not supply an exchangeability guarantee. The category-count analysis has quantified the separate obstacle faced by source-assisted certification. It has shown that, even with all category losses zero, optimistic multiplicity-free certification by a deterministic, uniformly valid, distribution-free 95% UCB requires at least 14, 29, and 59 iid category draws at α = 0.20 \alpha=0.20 , 0.10, and 0.05. The strict audit has provided only three or four certification categories, and even a certification-heavy reallocation with nonempty reference and proposal roles could provide at most 9 to 13. Category-unit CRESS has therefore returned τ ⋆ = 0 \tau^{\star}=0 throughout the 960 frozen configurations, consistent with the feasibility boundary rather than 960 independent statistical failures. By contrast, image-unit sensitivity analyses have selected positive thresholds in 36.7% to 60.3% of target cells under the idealized selected-mixture iid model, confirming that images and categories purchase evidence for different estimands. The resulting contribution is a practical study-design discipline: distinguish ranking from threshold reliability, identify attainable operating points, define the certification unit before evaluation, and match each guarantee to its estimand. Future work should evaluate category-rich source archives, real production shifts, temporal dependence, and condition-estimation error, and should investigate parametric, hierarchical, or side-information models whose additional assumptions are independently validated. Such work can convert the feasibility calculus developed here into more informative certification procedures without obscuring the distinction between image-mixture, marginal new-category, and category-conditional risk.

Distribution-Free Certification Limits for Few-Shot Anomaly Thresholds Gia Huy Thai 23120008@student.hcmus.edu.vn Nguyen Thai Anh anh.nt@vlu.edu.vn organization=University of Science, VNU-HCM, city=Ho Chi Minh City, country=Vietnam organization=Faculty of Information Technology, Van Lang School of Technology, Van Lang University, city=Ho Chi Minh City, country=Vietnam Abstract Few-shot anomaly detectors are judged by ranking metrics, yet deployment requires an alarm threshold with a controlled false-alarm rate (FAR). We ask how much normal evidence, in images or category units, is needed to certify such a threshold for an unseen category. Using a frozen DINOv2 principal component analysis (PCA) residual ranker on 15 MVTec and 12 VisA categories under four corruption types, we show that target-only leave-one-image-out (LOIO) calibration is resolution-limited and shift-fragile: rank values cannot fall below 1 / ( k + 1 ) 1/(k+1) , and at the attainable level α = 0.20 \alpha=0.20 , empirical FAR reaches 0.341 on Gaussian-corrupted MVTec at k = 4 k=4 , 1.7 times the nominal level. A category-count feasibility calculus is then derived: even with all-zero category losses and no multiplicity charged, any deterministic, uniformly valid, distribution-free 95% upper confidence bound (UCB) requires at least 14, 29, and 59 independent and identically distributed (iid) category draws at α = 0.20 \alpha=0.20 , 0.10 0.10 , and 0.05 0.05 ; these counts are necessary but not sufficient. The Cross-category Reliability Estimation with Source Support (CRESS) protocol splits source categories into disjoint reference, proposal, and certification roles. With only three or four certification categories, all 960 frozen configurations return the fail-closed threshold τ ⋆ = 0 \tau^{\star}=0 , and the smallest category-level UCB is 0.950. Image-unit analyses of the same archive select positive thresholds in 36.7% to 60.3% of target cells; these bounds hold for the selected source mixture, not for the marginal risk of a new-category draw. The contribution is a quantitative feasibility boundary and an estimand-aware protocol specifying when source evidence can, and cannot, support a transferable reliability claim. keywords Industrial anomaly detection ,Few-shot learning ,Conformal prediction ,Distribution-free certification ,Distribution shift ,Reliability † † corresponding: Corresponding author. 1 Introduction At the nominal false-alarm level α = 0.20 \alpha=0.20 , the target-only alarm evaluated in this study achieves an empirical false-alarm rate (FAR) of 0.341 on Gaussian-corrupted MVTec at k = 4 k=4 . This value represents the largest dataset-level aggregate in the frozen corruption grid and is approximately 1.7 times the intended level. This figure does not represent a population-level failure probability; rather, it is a benchmark observation pooled across categories and five support-sampling seeds under a single declared synthetic shift. However, this result highlights an operational discrepancy that ranking metrics alone do not capture. A detector may assign higher anomaly scores to defects than to normal images, resulting in a strong area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) or average precision (AP), yet a fixed score threshold can still yield substantially different false-alarm behavior across categories or input conditions. This discrepancy is especially significant in few-shot industrial anomaly detection (AD). Typically, a target category provides only k ∈ { 1 , 2 , 4 , 8 } k\in\{1,2,4,8\} known-normal support images, while anomalous examples are rare, heterogeneous, and unavailable for threshold calibration. Frozen visual foundation models enable ranking in this context: DINOv2 [ 24 ] patch features support nearest-neighbor (NN) memory banks, as implemented in PatchCore-style methods and AnomalyDINO [ 27 , 7 ] , or compact principal component analysis (PCA) normal subspaces, as in SubspaceAD [ 20 ] . However, these advances do not inherently determine which alarm threshold possesses a stable operational interpretation. Two primary responses are possible. The first is to calibrate on the k k target-normal support images. The target-only method evaluates each support image using a leave-one-image-out (LOIO) fit and ranks a test score against the resulting normal scores. This approach is label-free and interpretable, but its rank values are restricted to the grid { j / ( k + 1 ) } \{j/(k+1)\} . Increasing k k refines this grid; however, it does not guarantee that the support and shifted test scores meet the exchangeability conditions required for false-alarm validity. The empirical FAR of 0.341 illustrates this distinction: while the operating level is achievable, the shifted-normal rank distribution is anti-conservative compared to the exchangeable reference. The second approach involves leveraging normal evidence from non-target source categories. A larger source archive provides finer empirical ranks and enables the proposal of thresholds below those available in the target-only grid. However, this strategy alters the underlying statistical question. Independent image samples from a specified source mixture can estimate risk for that mixture, whereas a guarantee for a previously unseen category requires independent and identically distributed (iid) category units from a defined meta-population. Repeated images, corruption views, or support seeds do not constitute new category units. Consequently, the central question addressed in this paper is: How much source evidence, measured in which statistical unit, is needed to certify an anomaly threshold for a new category? We address this question at three levels. First, for any deterministic, uniformly valid, distribution-free 95% upper confidence bound (UCB) based solely on independent and identically distributed (iid) category losses, an all-zero sample cannot certify α = 0.20 \alpha=0.20 , 0.10, or 0.05 with fewer than 14, 29, or 59 categories, respectively, even without multiplicity. These values represent optimistic impossibility limits rather than sufficient sample sizes for the procedure. Under frozen simultaneous allocation, the corresponding lower limits are at least 22, 46, and 94 for a single candidate, while the declared Hoeffding rule requires 60, 240, and 958 categories, respectively. Second, we audit target-only normal rank values under four controlled corruptions and demonstrate that crossing the finite resolution floor does not guarantee a stable FAR. Third, we employ CRESS to partition source categories into disjoint reference, threshold-proposal, and certification roles and assess whether the available archive achieves the predicted feasibility boundary. CRESS functions as a source-assisted thresholding and audit protocol rather than as a novel anomaly ranker. The inherited ranking substrate is a frozen DINOv2 PCA residual. The reference categories establish a source-reference rank map, proposal categories define a finite candidate set, and certification categories evaluate fixed candidates using a family-adjusted UCB. The protocol outputs either the largest passing threshold or the fail-closed value of zero. Source-risk dominance enables the transfer of the bound to a specific target category. An iid category-sampling model provides only a marginal bound averaged over a new-category draw, rather than category-conditional control for each realized target. Neither normalization nor source pooling satisfies these requirements. The strict audit includes only three certification categories in VisA cells and four in MVTec and transfer cells. This limitation is not solely attributable to the fixed 0.50 / 0.25 / 0.25 0.50/0.25/0.25 split. The eligible source pools contain 11, 14, or 15 categories. Maintaining nonempty reference and proposal roles restricts certification categories to at most 9, 12, or 13, all below the optimistic 14-category threshold at α = 0.20 \alpha=0.20 . Consequently, category-unit certification assigns τ ⋆ = 0 \tau^{\star}=0 to every target cell across the 960 frozen configurations. This outcome does not represent 960 independent failures or a computational or optimization failure. The configurations cover various jobs, source-view modes, support sizes, nominal levels, and conditions but share the same category-count obstruction. Their value is to show that the fail-closed outcome persists throughout the declared grid in the regime where analytic calculations predict infeasibility. In contrast, under the idealized iid source-image model, image-unit analyses include 72 to 191 units per cell and select positive thresholds in 36.7% to 60.3% of target cells, depending on the source-to-target job. This contrast does not reflect a simple stronger-versus-weaker certificate; rather, the two analyses address different risk profiles. The same source archive is statistically large when measured in images but insufficient when deployment is considered at the category level. Patch distribution, self-supervised, and reconstruction-discriminative approaches such as PaDiM, CutPaste, and DRAEM provided important context for this literature [ 8 , 21 , 35 ] . PatchCore [ 27 ] established memory-bank patch retrieval as a robust baseline by storing representative normal features and scoring test patches using NN distance. AnomalyDINO [ 7 ] extended this paradigm to few-shot inspection with frozen DINOv2 representations. Subsequent work introduced registration-based adaptation (RegAD [ 15 ] ), graph-structured memory (GraphCore [ 32 ] ), and fast feature reconstruction (FastRecon [ 9 ] ). Vision-language methods included WinCLIP [ 16 ] , CLIP-SAM collaboration [ 22 ] , and cross-modal prompt regularization [ 31 ] . InCTRL introduced in-context residual learning [ 36 ] . These methods were effective rankers; however, their raw score scales did not, by construction, provide a certified false-alarm rate interpretation. Calibration under distribution shift is also known to degrade for deep models in general [ 25 ] . The present work is complementary: rather than competing on ranking, it examines how few-shot detectors should expose decision reliability. 2.2 Frozen-Feature Subspace Detectors Subspace approaches replaced explicit patch retrieval with a compact normal subspace. SubspaceAD [ 20 ] demonstrated that frozen DINOv2 patch features and PCA or subspace residuals were already effective for few-shot anomaly ranking, establishing the ranking mechanism as prior art. The present contribution begins after computing the residual and examines the reliability claims that a low-storage subspace detector can support under few-shot and distribution-shift conditions. 2.3 Calibration and Decision Reliability in Few-Shot AD Calibration measured agreement between predicted confidence and empirical correctness [ 26 , 11 ] . Standard post-hoc methods included Platt scaling and temperature scaling [ 26 , 11 ] . Histogram binning and isotonic regression provided nonparametric alternatives [ 33 , 34 ] . Sparse labels, open-ended anomaly types, and category-dependent scores made this objective especially difficult in AD. Prior reliability analyses of few-shot AD based on DINOv2 have also documented calibration and perturbation sensitivity [ 17 ] . These findings motivated our separation of ranking quality from the operational question of whether a declared alarm rule maintains its requested false-alarm behavior under a specified shift. A calibrated probability summary alone would not constitute such a risk guarantee. 2.4 Conformal Prediction and Risk-Controlled Calibration Conformal prediction transformed nonconformity scores into p-values under exchangeability assumptions [ 30 , 28 , 1 ] . This approach was particularly well suited for normal-only few-shot AD because normal support images defined a reference distribution without needing real anomalies. The literature on conformal AD was well established. Leave-one-out, bootstrap, and cross-conformal anomaly detectors had been directly analyzed [ 13 ] . Weighted conformal detection in low-data regimes examined the effects of resolution and effective sample size [ 14 ] . General nonconformity toolkits had been developed [ 12 ] . Few-shot conformal prediction with auxiliary tasks addressed the challenge of small target calibration sets [ 10 ] . Conformal AD, LOIO calibration, auxiliary-task transfer, and weighted conformal p-values were therefore established mechanisms. Risk-controlling calibration methods were developed before this work. The Learn then Test framework formulated finite-sample calibration as a multiple-testing problem over candidate configurations [ 2 ] . Conformal risk control selected parameters to control the expectation of a monotone loss [ 3 ] . In anomaly detection, PAC-Wrap provided semi-supervised probably approximately correct (PAC) bounds for false-positive and false-negative rates around a base detector [ 23 ] . These studies established general principles of candidate testing, held-out risk assessment, and one-sided error bounds. This work does not claim those statistical primitives as novel. Instead, CRESS applies these principles for normal-only cross-category thresholding by assigning disjoint source categories to reference, proposal, and certification roles. It distinguishes selected-mixture image risk from marginal new-category risk and audits whether the available category count can support a nonzero threshold under the declared iid model. Structure-aware conformal adaptation has also been studied outside the context of anomaly detection. Lam and Anh proposed Heterophily-Aware Diffused Conformal Prediction (HeAD-CP), which adapted graph-score diffusion using label-free local homophily estimates and showed that uniform diffusion could impair prediction-set efficiency on heterophilic graphs while preserving marginal coverage [ 18 ] . This result supported the broader need to audit reliability transformations under structural shift; however, its setting concerned graph neural network (GNN) node-classification sets rather than few-shot industrial anomaly alarms or cross-category source certification. The deterministic source-view choices were conceptually informed by the shared-versus-specialized selection motif in Shape-Adapting Gated Experts (SAGE) [ 29 ] . That work concerned learned expert selection rather than certification of anomaly thresholds. CRESS does not use a learned expert gate; its source-view modes are predeclared protocol choices, and its reference, proposal, and certification partitions have disjoint statistical roles. The citation therefore records design inspiration without attributing CRESS validity or novelty to the SAGE architecture. This contribution begins with the independent-category requirement of a simultaneous source certificate, using the target-only grid 1 / ( k + 1 ) 1/(k{+}1) as a motivating finite-resolution constraint. Established confidence tools are specialized into Hoeffding-specific and distribution-free all-zero category-budget calculations. Corruption-shift deviations are empirically audited. Source-assisted candidate thresholds are evaluated without target anomaly labels. CRESS does not introduce a new nonconformity score or generic confidence bound.
